title: Of thumbs
paragraphs: Tacitus reports that among certain barbarian kings, their custom for making a binding pledge was to join their right hands close together, interlace their thumbs, and when they had pressed hard enough for the blood to show at the tips, lightly pricked them with some sharp instrument and sucked each other's blood.

Physicians say the thumbs are the master fingers of the hand, and that their Latin name comes from "pollere", to be strong. The Greeks called them "antikheir", as if to say a second hand. And it seems the Latins also sometimes used the word in this sense, for the whole hand:
"Sed nec vocibus excitata blandis, Molli pollici nec rogata, surgit."
["Neither to be excited by soft words or by the thumb." — Mart., xii. 98, 8.]
In Rome it was a sign of favour to press the thumbs down and turn them in:
["Thy patron will applaud thy sport with both thumbs" — Horace.]
and a sign of disfavour to raise them and turn them out:
["The populace, with inverted thumbs, kill all that come before them." — Juvenal, iii. 36]

The Romans exempted from military service everyone maimed in the thumbs, on the ground that they no longer had enough strength to hold a weapon. Augustus confiscated the estate of a Roman knight who had maliciously cut off the thumbs of his two young sons to keep them out of the army; and before him, the Senate, during the Italian War, had sentenced Caius Vatienus to perpetual imprisonment and confiscated all his goods for having deliberately cut off his own left thumb to exempt himself from that campaign. Someone — I have forgotten who — after winning a sea battle, cut off the thumbs of all his beaten enemies to render them unable to fight or handle an oar. The Athenians also had the thumbs of the Aeginetans cut off, to deprive them of their advantage at sea.
In Lacedaemon, schoolmasters used to chastise their pupils by biting their thumbs.
